extracted.intended_audience: Citizens, voters, and state delegates considering the ratification and design of the proposed federal Constitution (late-18th-century American public)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and arguments for structuring the House of Representatives: election frequency/term length, apportionment rules, total number of representatives, and related procedural/functional considerations for a federal legislature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election frequency should bind representatives to constituents
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent elections are a means of binding representatives to their constituents; historically a triennial or biennial return has been deemed sufficient to preserve dependence of representatives on the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text surveys historical practice (Britain, Ireland, American colonies) and concludes that reducing septennial to triennial (or biennial under the federal system) increases popular influence; biennial elections cannot be dangerous to the requisite dependence of the House on constituents given the federal context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term length must be proportional to the legislative power held
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a legislative body holds greater power, its term/duration should be shorter; conversely, bodies with less power may safely have longer terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author applies the maxim to argue that because the federal legislature will possess only part of supreme legislative authority (unlike the British Parliament), somewhat longer terms (biennial rather than annual) are appropriate. The general principle: duration of office should inverse with magnitude of delegated power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed constitutional terms are more secure than mutable statutory terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Elections unalterably fixed by a constitution provide stronger security for liberty than elections that are frequent but subject to change by the ordinary power of government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay contrasts annual elections under a mutable government (where legislature can change terms) with biennial elections fixed by constitution; the latter is argued to better secure liberties because safeguards cannot be legislatively altered to extend terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term length should allow accumulation of requisite federal knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Members must have sufficient practical knowledge of the diverse laws, commerce, militia, treaties, and foreign policy relevant to federal legislation; the period of service should bear proportion to the knowledge required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal business is more novel and diversified than state business; some necessary knowledge (laws of different states, commercial usages, law of nations) is best acquired by practical attention while serving. Hence two-year terms better enable representatives to attain necessary competence than one-year terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical considerations (travel and logistics) justify longer terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Distance representatives must travel and arrangements required by that travel make longer terms (e.g., two years) less burdensome and more attractive to qualified persons than single-year terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long travel and expense may deter suitable candidates if service were limited to a single year; extending term length reduces this deterrent effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longer terms reduce incentives for spurious/illicit election returns
rubrics_metrics.description: If elections are very frequent (annual), the short time between elections makes it unattractive to investigate and annul spurious returns, encouraging unlawful means to obtain seats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because each house judges elections and qualifications and contested-return processes take time, a longer term lessens the benefit gained by illicit returns and thereby reduces such abuses, especially in distant states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment of representatives should be based on aggregate population
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of representatives allotted to each State ought to be regulated by population numbers (the same rule used for direct taxes), because numbers are the proper standard for representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although population is an imperfect measure of wealth (taxation), it is the least objectionable practicable rule for apportionment. The convention chose the same rule for representation and direct taxes to obtain a practicable and generally sanctioned measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compromise counting of slaves in apportionment (three-fifths)
rubrics_metrics.description: Slaves are to be regarded in a mixed character — partly persons and partly property — and for federal counting are to be considered as inhabitants but 'debased by servitude' (i.e., counted as three-fifths of a person).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay defends the constitutional compromise: slaves partake of both personhood and property under law (e.g., subject to protection and punishable), so treating them as three-fifths in the census is reasonable and necessary for Southern states' concurrence. Also notes that if state laws restored rights, slaves would then be fully persons for representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the same rule for representation and taxation to balance state incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the same census rule to both representation and taxation gives states opposed incentives that moderate exaggeration or reduction of population counts, encouraging impartiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If representation alone governed counts, states would be tempted to exaggerate inhabitants; if taxation alone, to undercount. Using a single rule for both purposes creates opposing interests that balance each other and promote fairer reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation should reflect both population and relative wealth/interests of states
rubrics_metrics.description: Because government protects both persons and property, some regard to property (wealth) in apportionment is defensible; larger, wealthier states have legitimate reasons to seek proportionate representation because states do not influence each other like wealthy individuals do within a state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues the federal system gives equal voting weight to each representative in the legislature; therefore, to secure advantages warranted by superior wealth and importance, states should obtain more representatives rather than rely on informal influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total number of representatives must balance deliberative function and avoidance of mob/confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be enough members to secure the benefits of free consultation and guard against improper combinations, yet not so many as to cause confusion, intemperance, or mob-like behavior; no fixed arithmetic ratio fits all states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different states have widely varying representative-to-population ratios; very small or very large assemblies have different trade-offs. The Constitution's initial size (65) with provision to increase by census (one per 30,000) is defended as reasonable, and growth over time will address early smallness concerns. The author rejects purely arithmetical rules and emphasizes judgment about minimum and maximum effective sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smaller initial representative bodies can be safe when powers are limited and external checks exist
rubrics_metrics.description: A comparatively small number (sixty-five initially) is not necessarily unsafe because the federal legislature's powers are limited and it will be watched by state legislatures and other branches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay contends that in the political temper of America and with state legislatures' oversight, the risk of a small House betraying liberties is low; census-based increases further mitigate long-term concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longer terms aid the practical inauguration and formation of the federal government and code
rubrics_metrics.description: The most laborious period will be inaugurating the government and drafting the primordial federal code; longer terms will ease this primeval task and make subsequent improvements easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early years will demand more work and continuity; improvements on initial drafts will be easier year-by-year, so longer representative terms facilitate continuity and institutional memory during critical foundational phases.
